“What I do is dance. But this dance comes from a culture, and that culture matters.” It was respect and appreciation for cultural life that, above all, drove Ford McKeown Larose to build a career on his love of this art. “I’m one of those kids who didn’t have much. I held on to dance. I couldn’t afford private lessons, and dance, hip-hop culture and street dance told me: ‘You don’t need all that.’ Headphones, your body and your imagination – that’s all you need. And thanks to that, today, I’m happy.”
Surnommé « The Mover », Ford s’est établ: Nicknamed “The Mover,” Ford has established himself in the art world as a committed and driven figure. Today, he runs his own dance company and frequently organizes free dance sessions in the neighbourhood where he grew up. Describing himself as a “Saint-Michel guy,” he hopes to contribute to the artistic development of young people in Montréal’s neighbourhoods.
Ford confie qu’au début de sa carrière a: Ford says that early in his artistic career, his daily life was marked by ups and downs. While his motivation was at its peak when he decided to devote himself fully to dance, he also remembers the difficult reality he had to overcome. “I went through a huge number of stages. At the start, it was fine, a lot of opportunities came up. But I quickly had to adapt to life as a self-employed worker. I had just quit school, and I found myself alone, having to manage everything with no economic or financial education.”
Perdu dans cette nouvelle réalité qu’il: Lost in this new reality that he struggled to tame, the ambitious young dancer nonetheless found ways to get by in every situation. “When I started negotiating my first contracts, I remembered my parents always haggling whenever we went to the flea market. That’s when I understood why it was important to them, and why I had to know how to fend for myself, know my worth and never let others devalue me,” he says of the resourcefulness he developed early on.
Parti sur une belle lancée, Ford raconte: Off to a good start, Ford says that a few problems still stood in his way. “First there was a culture clash. When I started working, I was mostly given teaching contracts. I taught mainly outside the city, in places like Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Chambly, Blainville, and so on. I was leaving Montréal a lot. I’m a Saint-Michel guy. I wasn’t used to leaving the neighbourhood, let alone the city,” Ford recalls. Speaking about the cultural differences he had to deal with while teaching far from the metropolis, he adds: “Going from Saint-Michel to Valleyfield was a big change for me. I found myself in the middle of a purely Québécois culture, which wasn’t very present in Montréal.”
Être un adolescent ou un jeune adulte et: Being a teenager or a young adult living in Saint-Michel in a first-generation immigrant family is a reality that has often clashed with the dream of practising your art and being able to live from it. By betting on his dream and drawing on his determination to achieve great things, Ford managed to escape the reality he thought he was condemned to.
C’est vers 15 ans que Ford commence à se: Around age 15, Ford began to question things. He explains that, between school and church, there was no cultural or artistic life in his world. And as a teenager, his family life was rather oppressive. “Often, immigrant parents don’t have access to jobs that allow them to live with dignity. They have to limit themselves, they have very little fun… Even if they want something else for their children, I felt shut in.” The pressure Ford felt pushed him to question his path. That’s where his desire for freedom was born.
« Mon désir de liberté, c’est ce qui m’a: “My desire for freedom is what brought me to dance,” the dancer continues. “In 2007, I came across a video of a dancer who inspired me. His message was very much about freedom and dance; and at that time, that’s what I needed.” Speaking of his search for emancipation and freedom, Ford says that dance did indeed fulfil him.
Après la découverte de la danse suivent: After he discovered dance, a series of twists and turns followed. “Dance was always in the back of my mind. I was dancing all the time.” Dance thus took a dominant place in the young Saint-Michel resident’s life, following him into his daily activities. “I even found myself dancing in class. I’d see my teachers turn around and look at me, probably thinking I was crazy. At CEGEP, people even recognized me and would come up to me and say: ‘You’re the guy who dances!’”
« Plus le temps passait, plus je me conc: “As time went by, I focused more and more on dance,” Ford recounts. As he grew up, his mind turned increasingly toward a lifestyle centred on this art. His interest in dance dates back to adolescence, but it was when classes were suspended in 2012 (during the Maple Spring in Quebec) that Ford finally saw a concrete opportunity to start devoting himself more seriously to dance. “There were no classes for nine months. I finally had a valid excuse to dance, and I could take advantage of it. When the strike ended, it was clear in my head, there was no turning back.” After this revelation, the young Montrealer summoned his courage and confronted his mother about it. “I told her I was quitting school. It was a difficult and violent conversation. She didn’t agree at all, but over time, I proved to her that it could work,” he adds.
Faire de sa passion son métier a été la: Making a living from his passion was the main reason Ford got into dance. But why stop there? Eager to have a real impact on society, the young man decided to go further. “The goal was to gain a certain recognition so I could have a credible effect on others,” he explains. “That’s why a partner and I decided to start our own dance company. By investing all that time and all that money, we earned the recognition we needed to actually help and give back to young people who were deprived of a certain artistic culture,” adds the Haitian-born entrepreneur.
Mais pourquoi un tel intérêt pour les je: But why such an interest in young people from the neighbourhoods? Whether in his home neighbourhood – Saint-Michel – or in other neglected Montréal neighbourhoods, Ford says he sees himself in all those young people who lack motivation. Inspired by his own experience as a young racialized person, he says: “When you step out of your house and you see people, you really get the feeling that people aren’t living, they’re surviving. Young people feel that the only ones who make it are rappers or athletes. They think it’s one of the only ways to really make it out.” Ford points out that there are many other careers, less “trendy” than some, that young people often tend to forget or overlook, but that are just as relevant. “We have talented artists and musicians in our cultures who are invisible. We need to put them forward so young people can be inspired and motivated. That way, they can see themselves in them and tell themselves that they can succeed too if they want to.”
« Les jeunes peuvent réussir s’ils le ve: “Young people can succeed if they want to,” repeats the man known as “The Mover.” “When I talk about giving back, I don’t want to change what young people are interested in. I want to help them put in the work needed for what they love so that it leads to something in the end.” He also wants to show that there is success in the artistic circles of the neighbourhoods. “When there are people living their best life thanks to their own work, others can tell themselves they’ll do the same. By giving back my passion for dance to them, I pass on that message, whatever young people’s interests are,” he adds. Drawing on his own experience, Ford underlines the need for initiatives like his: “By teaching young people, I realized that I myself would have wanted access to someone like that.”
<strong>La réalité du milieu artistique: The reality of the arts scene for young people
En revenant sur l’importance de la vie c: Returning to the importance of cultural and artistic life for young Montrealers, the professional dancer insists on the need to invest in local talent. “A large share of young people follow or see Montréal dancers and artists on social media, but don’t know they’re from here. For them, and for many others, anything good has to come from the United States or somewhere else.” It is this lack of recognition of the quality and potential of local youth, especially those from the neighbourhoods, where artistic life is less vibrant, that slows young people’s inclusion in the arts scene. “In Montréal, we don’t have many promotional platforms for artists who look like us. That’s also why young people decide to look elsewhere,” he laments.
Ford estime que, pour changer les choses: Ford believes that, to change things, you have to work directly with young people. “I work a lot in Saint-Michel, because that’s where I’m from,” he says. “It’s a neighbourhood with realities very similar to those of neighbourhoods in the United States. These are also the same neighbourhoods that the dances I teach come from. In Montréal’s elementary and high schools, kids dance what’s trendy – so it’s part of the reality of young people in the neighbourhoods.”
Si elle représente quelque chose de diff: While it means something different to everyone, dance does have an impact on young people’s lives. It’s even beneficial for those who don’t have a foot in the artistic and cultural world. “The Mover” has managed to reconcile his passion with his reality as a young child of immigrants in Saint-Michel, while being able to give back to his community through his personal accomplishments.
Sachant, tout au long de son développeme: Aware throughout his development that his identity as a young person from the neighbourhood could clash with his reality as a dancer, Ford nonetheless managed to create his own universe, and he hopes to help and inspire the next generation to understand that it’s a real possibility. “Really, I’m just a guy from the neighbourhood who believed in something, and it worked,” concludes the dancer, a smile at the corner of his lips.”
Son entrée dans le monde professionnel,: His entry into the professional world, driven by his desire to achieve what few young people from the neighbourhoods had managed to do, was quickly caught up by reality. While the joys of being independent allowed him to satisfy his need for emancipation, the young dancer from Saint-Michel still went through some less positive episodes. “When I started working with big companies and arts institutions, I experienced a lot of microaggressions. I felt it throughout my career, whether it was little words or implicit comments. Most of the people who work in this field are white; when you're a Black person, you can't put yourself in the position of a beggar, you always have to work twice as hard,” he says. Pursuing a career fuelled by his passion, Ford confides: “Making a living from your art means getting a lot of different pieces to fit together. It's a real awakening, and I understood that very quickly. If I'd come from a different background, the story would have been different. But since I come from a modest family, I had to figure things out on my own.” He is a reminder that behind his accomplishments lies a story shaped by the reality of his lived experience.
